samples.question: The picture shows four clips on a plain page, arranged in one tight two-by-two cluster: upper-left, upper-right, lower-left and lower-right of that cluster. A clip is two separate rows of small solid squares, an upper row and a lower row, with a clear empty gap between them and no mark joining them. The squares of both rows of a clip stand on the same eight evenly spaced column positions of that clip, so every square of the lower row sits directly below one column position of the upper row. Each of the eight columns of a clip therefore holds one square, two squares stacked one above the other, or no square at all: a column is covered once when exactly one of the clip's two rows has a square there, covered twice when both rows have a square there, and left bare when neither row has one. Every clip contains exactly eight squares in total, so the four clips carry exactly the same amount of ink and the same number of squares, and counting squares can never name a clip. Exactly one clip has all eight of its columns covered exactly once. Every other clip has at least one doubly covered column and exactly as many bare columns as doubly covered ones. Both rows of a clip must be read together: one row on its own never decides anything, and the leftmost and the rightmost column of every clip, including the losing ones, are always covered exactly once. The ink colours, which row of a clip holds more squares, the small sideways and up-and-down shifts of the clips, where the cluster sits on the page, and the tiny isolated specks dotted about the background all carry no information. Which clip of the cluster has every one of its eight columns covered by exactly one square? Answer with one of: upper-left, upper-right, lower-left, lower-right.
